hook.text: Central banks don't serve ordinary people. They serve banks. The Federal Reserve is JPMorgan's bank.

buildup.text: Commercial banks hold reserve accounts at the central bank, just like you hold an account at a commercial bank.

discovery.text: Central banks clear interbank payments, set reserve requirements, and provide emergency loans.

twist.text: Before central banks, banking panics happened regularly.

climax.text: Central banks exist because banking systems need a backstop. Someone has to be the bank that never runs out of money.

punchline.text: The bank's bank. Central banks backstop the entire financial system.

quiz.question: Who are central banks' primary customers?

hook.text: In 2022, US inflation hit 9.1%. The Fed raised interest rates from 0% to 5.25% in 16 months to slow it down.

buildup.text: When prices rise too fast, central banks raise rates. Higher rates make borrowing expensive.

discovery.text: The Fed targets 2% annual inflation. Not zero, because mild inflation encourages spending.

twist.text: Rate hikes take 12-18 months to fully work. By the time they do, the economy may have already slowed too much.

climax.text: Central banks fight inflation with a blunt tool: interest rates. The results are powerful but delayed and imprecise.

punchline.text: 0% to 5.25% in 16 months. The Fed's blunt hammer against inflation.

quiz.question: What inflation target does the Federal Reserve use?

hook.text: The Fed has a dual mandate: stable prices and maximum employment. Most central banks only target inflation.

buildup.text: When unemployment rises, the Fed cuts rates to stimulate borrowing, spending, and hiring. Cheap money creates jobs.

discovery.text: There's a tension: low unemployment can cause inflation, and fighting inflation can cause unemployment.

twist.text: The Phillips Curve looked stable until stagflation proved unemployment and inflation can rise together.

climax.text: Central banks influence employment through interest rates, but they can't create jobs directly.

punchline.text: Stable prices and full employment. The Fed's impossible balancing act.

quiz.question: What is the Fed's dual mandate?

hook.text: Central banks create money digitally. The Fed added $4.8 trillion during COVID by typing numbers into a computer.

buildup.text: When the Fed buys bonds, it credits the seller's bank account with new money.

discovery.text: This is called quantitative easing. The Fed doesn't print paper bills. It creates digital reserves that banks can lend.

twist.text: Money creation doesn't automatically cause inflation. If banks don't lend the new reserves, prices don't rise.

climax.text: Central banks have the power to create unlimited money.

punchline.text: $4.8 trillion created digitally. Not printed — typed into existence.

quiz.question: How did the Fed create money during COVID?
options: Digitally credited bank reserves through bond purchases

hook.text: In March 2020, financial markets froze. The Fed stepped in within days, lending $2 trillion to keep the system alive.

buildup.text: Central banks monitor systemic risk. They watch for signs that a failing bank or market could trigger wider collapse.

discovery.text: Stress tests simulate crises before they happen. Banks must prove they can survive a severe recession to keep operating.

twist.text: Markets expect central bank rescues. The 'Fed put' encourages risk-taking because traders assume a safety net exists.

climax.text: Stability is the central bank's unwritten mandate. Markets function only because everyone believes the backstop exists.

punchline.text: $2 trillion in days. Central banks keep the financial system breathing.

quiz.question: What is the 'Fed put'?
options: The market expectation that the Fed will rescue markets in a crisis

hook.text: Eight times a year, the Fed meets to decide interest rates. Markets move billions on every word of the announcement.

buildup.text: The federal funds rate is the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Fed controls this rate directly.

discovery.text: When the Fed changes this rate, every other rate follows: mortgages, car loans, credit cards, and savings accounts.

twist.text: The Fed doesn't set rates by law. It uses open market operations to push the rate where it wants.

climax.text: One number set eight times a year controls the cost of money for the entire economy. That's extraordinary power.

punchline.text: Eight meetings, one rate. It controls the cost of borrowing for everyone.

quiz.question: How often does the Fed meet to set interest rates?

hook.text: When rates hit zero, central banks can't cut further. So they invented QE: buying bonds to pump money into markets.

buildup.text: The Fed buys government bonds from banks. Banks get cash. The idea is they'll lend it out and stimulate the economy.

discovery.text: QE lowered long-term interest rates and boosted asset prices.

twist.text: QE primarily helped asset owners. If you owned stocks or property, you got richer.

climax.text: QE saved the economy but widened inequality. The rich got richer because they owned the assets that QE inflated.

punchline.text: Rates hit zero. QE pumped trillions into markets. Asset owners won most.

quiz.question: What is quantitative easing?
options: Central banks buying bonds to inject money into the economy

hook.text: Banks used to be required to keep 10% of deposits in reserve. In 2020, the Fed dropped that requirement to zero.

buildup.text: Reserve requirements limit how much banks can lend. Higher reserves mean less lending.

discovery.text: With zero reserves required, banks can theoretically lend every dollar deposited.

twist.text: China's central bank actively uses reserve ratios. It adjusts them to control lending in ways the Fed no longer does.

climax.text: Reserve requirements were banking's oldest control lever.

punchline.text: Reserve requirement: zero. The Fed now uses other tools to control banks.

quiz.question: What is the current US bank reserve requirement?

hook.text: Central banks discovered they can move markets just by talking. Forward guidance is monetary policy through words alone.

buildup.text: When the Fed says rates will stay low 'for an extended period,' businesses invest and consumers borrow on that promise.

discovery.text: Expectations shape behavior. By telling markets what's coming.

twist.text: In 2021, the Fed kept calling inflation 'transitory.' Markets believed them and didn't prepare. The guidance was wrong.

climax.text: Forward guidance is powerful when correct and dangerous when wrong.

punchline.text: Words move markets. But wrong words destroy credibility.

quiz.question: What is forward guidance?
options: Central bank communication about future policy intentions

hook.text: Japan and Europe charged banks to hold deposits. Negative rates mean you pay the bank to store your money.

buildup.text: The European Central Bank set its rate to -0.5% in 2019. Banks were penalized for parking cash instead of lending it.

discovery.text: The goal was to make idle reserves expensive, pushing banks and investors to keep money circulating.

twist.text: Banks didn't fully pass negative rates to depositors. They feared customers would withdraw cash and store it in safes.

climax.text: Negative rates proved there's a floor. People will hoard physical cash before accepting being charged to save.

punchline.text: Pay to save. Negative rates hit a wall when people choose cash.

quiz.question: Why did central banks implement negative interest rates?
options: To force banks to lend instead of hoarding cash

hook.text: The Fed isn't one bank. It's 12 regional reserve banks plus a Board of Governors in Washington.

buildup.text: The Board of Governors has 7 members appointed by the president.

discovery.text: The FOMC, which sets rates, has 12 voting members: all 7 governors plus 5 rotating reserve bank presidents.

twist.text: Regional reserve banks are technically private. Their boards include commercial bankers.

climax.text: The Fed is half public, half private, and entirely powerful.

punchline.text: 12 banks, 7 governors, one rate. The Fed was built on compromise.

quiz.question: How many regional reserve banks make up the Federal Reserve System?

topics.title: The Power of the Fed Chair

hook.text: The Fed Chair is often called the most powerful person in the world economy.

buildup.text: The Chair leads FOMC meetings, sets the agenda, and builds consensus among governors and bank presidents.

discovery.text: Greenspan, Bernanke, Yellen, and Powell each shaped decades of economic policy from this single position.

twist.text: The Chair serves 4-year terms but can be reappointed. Presidents can't fire the Chair.

climax.text: One unelected official controls interest rates for the world's largest economy.

punchline.text: One person, one speech, trillions moved.

quiz.question: Can the US President fire the Fed Chair?
options: No, the Chair serves fixed terms with independence from the President

hook.text: The Fed's balance sheet reached $8.9 trillion in 2022. It holds more assets than the GDP of Germany and Japan combined.

buildup.text: Before 2008, the balance sheet was under $1 trillion. QE from the financial crisis and COVID inflated it to $9 trillion.

discovery.text: The Fed holds mostly US Treasury bonds and mortgage-backed securities. It's the largest holder of US government debt.

twist.text: Shrinking the balance sheet (quantitative tightening) risks destabilizing markets.

climax.text: $9 trillion is easy to accumulate and hard to reduce. The Fed's balance sheet may never return to pre-crisis levels.

punchline.text: From $1 trillion to $9 trillion. Easy to inflate. Impossible to fully unwind.

quiz.question: What is the Fed's balance sheet primarily composed of?
options: US Treasury bonds and mortgage-backed securities

hook.text: Banks in trouble can borrow directly from the Fed's discount window.

buildup.text: The discount rate is set slightly above the federal funds rate.

discovery.text: The discount window prevents solvent banks from failing due to temporary cash shortages. It's liquidity insurance.

twist.text: Banks avoid the discount window because markets interpret its use as distress.

climax.text: A safety net nobody wants to use has limited value. The stigma of the discount window undermines its purpose.

punchline.text: Emergency cash available. But using it tells the world your bank is in trouble.

quiz.question: Why do banks avoid using the Fed's discount window?
options: Using it signals financial distress to the market

hook.text: Presidents have publicly pressured the Fed to cut rates.

buildup.text: In the 1970s, Nixon pressured Fed Chair Arthur Burns to keep rates low before the election. Inflation surged to 12%.

discovery.text: Central bank independence means politicians can't force rate changes.

twist.text: Turkey's president fired central bank governors who raised rates. Inflation soared to 85%.

climax.text: Every country that sacrificed central bank independence paid the price in inflation.

punchline.text: Pressure the central bank. Get short-term gain and long-term inflation.

quiz.question: What happened when Turkey's president fired central bank governors?

hook.text: The ECB sets monetary policy for 20 countries using one currency.

buildup.text: Created in 1998, the ECB manages the euro. Its primary mandate is price stability, targeting inflation near 2%.

discovery.text: The ECB's Governing Council has 26 members: 6 Executive Board members and 20 national central bank governors.

twist.text: What's right for Germany's economy is often wrong for Greece's.

climax.text: The ECB manages a monetary union without a fiscal union. One currency, 20 budgets, and no easy way to reconcile them.

punchline.text: One rate for 20 economies. The ECB manages an impossible compromise.

quiz.question: How many countries does the ECB set monetary policy for?

hook.text: Japan has fought deflation for 30 years. The Bank of Japan tried zero rates, negative rates, and QE.

buildup.text: Japan's bubble burst in 1990. Prices and wages stagnated for decades.

discovery.text: The BOJ pioneered QE in 2001, before any other central bank.

twist.text: The BOJ owns over 50% of Japanese government bonds. It effectively funds the government by buying its debt.

climax.text: Japan showed what happens when deflation takes hold. Central banks can create money but can't always create inflation.

punchline.text: 30 years of deflation. Japan proved money printing has limits.

quiz.question: What percentage of Japanese government bonds does the BOJ own?

hook.text: China's central bank controls the world's second-largest economy.

buildup.text: The PBOC manages interest rates, reserve requirements, and the yuan's exchange rate.

discovery.text: The PBOC uses 'window guidance': informal instructions to banks about how much to lend and to whom.

twist.text: China's managed exchange rate keeps the yuan artificially competitive.

climax.text: China's central bank is the most interventionist in the world.

punchline.text: Party-controlled central bank. China manages money supply, lending.

quiz.question: How much does the PBOC hold in foreign reserves?

hook.text: Switzerland's central bank owns $150 billion in US stocks. It's a major shareholder in Apple, Microsoft, and Amazon.

buildup.text: The SNB buys foreign assets to weaken the Swiss franc. A strong franc hurts Swiss exporters like Nestlé and Rolex.

discovery.text: By selling francs and buying dollars, euros, and stocks, the SNB pushes its currency down.

twist.text: Unlike the Fed, the SNB is publicly traded. You can buy shares in Switzerland's central bank on the stock exchange.

climax.text: A central bank that owns tech stocks and trades on a stock exchange.

punchline.text: Owns Apple stock. Traded on an exchange. Switzerland's central bank is unique.

quiz.question: Why does the Swiss National Bank buy US stocks?
options: To weaken the Swiss franc by selling it for foreign assets

hook.text: Nigeria, Argentina, and Turkey battled inflation above 50% while their central banks fought to maintain credibility.

buildup.text: Emerging market central banks face unique pressures: volatile currencies, capital flight, and political interference.

discovery.text: Many hold large dollar reserves to defend their currency.

twist.text: Argentina has had 10 currencies since 1970. Each new one was the central bank admitting the previous currency failed.

climax.text: Central banking in emerging markets is a constant fight for credibility. Without trust, no monetary tool works.

punchline.text: 10 currencies in 50 years. Argentina shows what happens when trust collapses.

quiz.question: How many different currencies has Argentina had since 1970?

hook.text: After QE, US household wealth rose $40 trillion. But 70% went to the richest 20% who owned stocks and property.

buildup.text: QE works by raising asset prices. If you own assets, you get richer. If you don't, you watch others pull ahead.

discovery.text: Home prices rose 40% during QE. First-time buyers were priced out while homeowners gained hundreds of thousands.

twist.text: Central banks say QE was necessary to prevent depression.

climax.text: QE saved the economy but widened the gap. The monetary medicine worked for the system but the side effects were unequal.

punchline.text: $40 trillion in new wealth. 70% went to the richest fifth of America.

quiz.question: Who benefited most from quantitative easing?

hook.text: In 2021, the Fed called inflation 'transitory' and kept rates at zero. It lasted 18 months and peaked at 9.1%.

buildup.text: Pandemic stimulus checks, supply chain disruptions, and low rates fueled spending.

discovery.text: The Fed delayed rate hikes by months, believing inflation would fade. By the time they acted, it had become entrenched.

twist.text: The delay forced the fastest rate hikes in 40 years. A gradual adjustment became an emergency response.

climax.text: Calling inflation transitory was the Fed's biggest recent mistake.

punchline.text: Called it transitory. Waited too long. Then raised rates at record speed.

quiz.question: What did the Fed call inflation in 2021?

topics.title: Too Big to Fail Moral Hazard

hook.text: In 2008, the government rescued big banks but let small ones fail.

buildup.text: AIG, Citigroup, and Bank of America received billions in bailouts.

discovery.text: Too-big-to-fail banks borrow at lower rates because lenders know the government will bail them out.

twist.text: Banks that received bailouts in 2008 are even bigger now.

climax.text: Bailouts create moral hazard. Each rescue encourages bigger bets because the cost of failure falls on taxpayers.

punchline.text: Bailed out in 2008. Even bigger now. The moral hazard loop continues.

quiz.question: What is the 'too big to fail' problem?
options: Large banks being rescued because their failure would crash the economy

hook.text: Should central banks fight climate change? The ECB and Bank of England say yes. The Fed says it's not their job.

buildup.text: The ECB now considers climate risk in its bond purchases. It buys fewer bonds from heavy carbon emitters.

discovery.text: Climate change creates financial risk: stranded assets, extreme weather losses.

twist.text: Critics argue central banks should stick to inflation and employment.

climax.text: As climate risk becomes financial risk, central banks are drawn in.

punchline.text: Climate risk is financial risk. Central banks are getting involved regardless.

quiz.question: How does the ECB address climate change?
options: It considers climate risk in bond purchases

hook.text: Bitcoin was created to bypass central banks. Its white paper says: 'A peer-to-peer electronic cash system'.

buildup.text: Crypto advocates argue central banks debase currency through printing.

discovery.text: Central banks view crypto as a threat to monetary sovereignty.

twist.text: China banned crypto entirely. The US is regulating it. No major central bank is willing to cede monetary control.

climax.text: The crypto vs. central bank battle is a contest over who controls money.

punchline.text: Crypto challenged central banks. They're fighting back with regulation.

quiz.question: Why do central banks view cryptocurrency as a threat?
options: It could undermine their ability to control monetary policy

hook.text: Over 130 countries are developing central bank digital currencies.

buildup.text: CBDCs would let citizens hold accounts directly at the central bank. No commercial bank needed as an intermediary.

discovery.text: Instant, free payments between anyone with a CBDC wallet. No Visa, no Swift, no clearing delays.

twist.text: CBDCs give governments total visibility into spending. Every transaction recorded.

climax.text: CBDCs offer efficiency at the cost of privacy. The future of money depends on how that tradeoff is resolved.

punchline.text: 130 countries exploring digital money. Efficiency vs. privacy is the battle.

quiz.question: What is a major concern about CBDCs?
options: Governments could track every transaction, eliminating financial privacy

hook.text: Central banks are experimenting with AI to predict inflation, detect fraud.

buildup.text: The Fed uses machine learning to analyze satellite images, credit card data.

discovery.text: AI could make monetary policy faster and more precise. Real-time data processing beats quarterly reports.

twist.text: Faster models can still misread noisy data, and a black-box mistake can distort policy at scale.

climax.text: AI will assist central bankers but not replace them. Monetary policy requires judgment algorithms can't yet provide.

punchline.text: AI assists, not decides. Central banking still needs human judgment.

quiz.question: How are central banks using AI?
options: To analyze data, predict inflation, and detect fraud

hook.text: The ECB ran climate stress tests in 2022. Two-thirds of eurozone banks had no framework for measuring climate risk.

buildup.text: Climate stress tests simulate how banks would survive extreme weather events, carbon taxes, and energy transitions.

discovery.text: Banks with heavy fossil fuel exposure face stranded assets.

twist.text: Banks are slow to reduce fossil fuel lending because it's currently profitable.

climax.text: Central banks can force banks to measure climate risk. Making them act on it is the harder challenge.

punchline.text: Two-thirds of banks unprepared. Climate risk is the next banking blind spot.

quiz.question: What did the ECB's climate stress tests reveal?
options: Two-thirds had no framework for measuring climate risk

hook.text: Sweden is 98% cashless. Cash use has fallen below 1% of transactions.

buildup.text: Digital payments are faster, trackable, and cheaper. Businesses prefer cards because cash handling costs 1-2% of sales.

discovery.text: As cash disappears, central banks lose a direct connection to citizens.

twist.text: Cashless societies exclude the unbanked. 4.5% of US households have no bank account.

climax.text: Cash is freedom from surveillance and banking requirements.

punchline.text: 98% cashless in Sweden. But 4.5% of Americans have no bank account.

quiz.question: What percentage of transactions in Sweden use cash?

hook.text: Crypto, CBDCs, and fintech challenge the central bank model.

buildup.text: Central banks survived two world wars, the Great Depression, the 2008 crisis, and COVID.

discovery.text: No institution can replace the central bank as lender of last resort.

twist.text: Central banks may evolve from rate-setters to platform operators.

climax.text: Central banks will survive by adapting. Their form may change, but the function — controlling money — is here to stay.

punchline.text: 330 years and counting. Central banks evolve. They don't disappear.

quiz.question: Why are central banks likely to survive technological disruption?
options: No alternative can serve as lender of last resort with unlimited money creation
